usage.title: Invalid Pairings
usage.subtitle: Explicit invalid token combinations that break role logic, semantic coherence, contrast integrity, or accessibility behavior.
rows: Neutral, subtle, and other low-emphasis surface contexts, such as canvas layers, default surfaces, or subtle semantic backgrounds
On-color foregrounds are reserved for strong fills and other high-emphasis colored surfaces. Using them on neutral or subtle surfaces breaks role intent and weakens readable hierarchy
High-emphasis colored surfaces, such as branded fills, strong intent backgrounds, or critical status containers
Base text and icon tokens are not the default foreground treatment for strong fills. High-emphasis surfaces require dedicated on-color foregrounds to preserve contrast and role consistency
Reversed-contrast surfaces, such as inverse containers, dark overlays, or inverted regions
Inverse surfaces require inverse foreground treatment. Default text and icon tokens break reversed-contrast logic and create inconsistent theme behavior
Reversed-contrast structural contexts, such as inverse cards, dark sections, or elevated inverse containers
Inverse surfaces require inverse border treatment. Default neutral borders can lose edge clarity and weaken structural separation
Standard light-surface contexts, such as canvas, neutral containers, or default cards
Inverse tokens are reserved for reversed-contrast contexts. Using them on standard surfaces creates false inversion and disrupts visual hierarchy
High-emphasis structural separation, such as strong semantic fills, branded blocks, or critical banners
Subtle neutral borders do not provide sufficient separation on high-emphasis fills. Use inverse or validated semantic border treatment where structure must remain visible
Neutral structural framing, such as layout grouping, card boundaries, or default field outlines
Intent borders are semantic signals, not structural separators. Using them as default UI framing injects unintended meaning into neutral states
Long-form primary reading contexts, such as body copy, page text, or persistent product content and decorative or default UI icons
Intent fg tokens are semantic accents, not default reading or icon colors. Using them as primary body content or default icons overloads meaning and reduces signal clarity
Any intent token with conflicting semantic meaning
Semantic surfaces with a different meaning, such as positive content on negative backgrounds or warning icons in info containers
Cross-intent pairings break semantic coherence. A token family must not communicate one meaning while the surrounding surface communicates another
Depth and interaction layers, such as overlays, scrims, or modal backdrops
Overlay surfaces are depth and interaction layers, not readable content surfaces. Content must be placed on a dedicated container above the overlay
Enabled, interactive, or standard hierarchy contexts, such as active controls, default content, or selectable UI
Disabled tokens indicate non-availability, not reduced emphasis. Using them outside disabled states weakens hierarchy and misrepresents interactivity
High-emphasis colored surfaces, such as strong fills, branded actions, or critical semantic regions

Standard light-surface contexts, such as default forms, neutral cards, or page-level containers
Inverse focus is reserved for dark or strong-fill contexts. On standard surfaces it introduces unnecessary emphasis and breaks focus consistency
Non-destructive interaction contexts, such as primary actions, neutral controls, or standard navigation
Negative focus is reserved for destructive interactive contexts. Using it elsewhere introduces false severity and breaks semantic trust
